cards.title: Distinguish Cross-Sells (complementary product) from Upsells (more of the same)
cards.summary: Cross-sells offer a different complementary product while upsells sell a larger/multi-pack quantity of the item already in the cart, and each fits a different catalog.
cards.use_when: Designing the in-cart, checkout or post-purchase add-on step for a product page or bundle decision.
steps: Classify your add-on offer before building it: a cross-sell is a different complementary product bought alongside the main item (e.g., buy the t-shirt, offer matching socks or shorts); an upsell is more of the same product (e.g., buying a 1-month supply and offering a discounted 3-month supply).

Match the mechanic to your catalog: cross-sells suit multi-SKU brands because you can sell into other products; upsells suit single-hero-SKU brands because you are just moving customers up a quantity ladder.
Treat both as sitting downstream from the primary front-end offer, not as part of it — they only show after the main purchase decision is made.

For each candidate add-on, calculate the take rate (share of exposed customers who accept), the dollar value added, and the gross margin of the added item, because all three drive the outcome and none should be optimized alone.
caveats: The source treats these as post-decision add-ons; pushing them too early (while the buyer is still deciding) risks reducing the primary conversion.
Terminology is the presenter's definition — align your team on it so reporting is consistent.

cards.title: Optimize upsells/cross-sells on incremental contribution profit, not take rate alone
cards.summary: The correct upsell is the one maximizing take rate times added AOV times gross margin, which often means a lower-take-rate, higher-margin item wins.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product to place as the in-cart or post-purchase upsell/cross-sell.
steps: Use the formula: incremental contribution profit per order = take rate % × average order value of the added item × contribution/gross margin %.
Compute it for each candidate rather than judging by any single metric. Worked example: 10% take rate × $50 item × 50% margin = $2.50 incremental CP per order.

Compare candidates at the same stage. Example from the source: upsell A has 20% take rate, $40 AOV lift, 30% margin (≈$2.40) versus upsell B with 10% take rate, $30 AOV lift, 60% margin (≈$1.80) — A wins here, but the source's counterexample shows B can win when A's discount erodes margin, so always run the numbers rather than assuming.
Don't default to pushing your highest-margin product — congruence with what the customer bought drives take rate, and a better-fit lower-margin item can still net more.
At the point of the add-on the order is already committed, so any positive contribution is incremental and can justify a higher customer acquisition cost.
caveats: Illustrative numbers from the source; your take rates and margins will differ — measure your own.
For in-cart upsells specifically, the source advises measuring success by gross margin lift rather than AOV lift, to avoid over-favoring low-margin SKs.

cards.title: Match add-on placement to friction level and expected take rate
cards.summary: Cart, checkout and post-purchase add-ons carry very different friction and take rates, so the offer type should change by placement.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to place an upsell or cross-sell (cart drawer, checkout, or post-purchase page).
steps: In-cart has medium friction (buyer still deciding): typical take rates are around 5–15% per the source. Use threshold unlocks (e.g., 'add one more for X'), samples, or a complimentary product at a spend threshold.

At checkout, friction rises counterintuitively because the buyer has already committed to the order and price — take rates decline. Avoid selling another product; instead offer a low-friction add-on such as shipping protection (source example: ~$4.99 with ~30% take rate and near-100% margin because refunds are rare and often covered by the carrier).
Post-purchase has near-zero friction when set up as a one-click charge — the source says always have one. Take rates can reach 35–40% in some cases.
Layer post-purchase offers in sequence: first offer, then a second offer to those who took the first, each with its own take rate (source example: 25% then 10%).
Pick the placement per product and audience, then A/B test to validate the take rate.
caveats: The 5–15%, 30%, 35–40% figures are the source's observed examples, not guaranteed benchmarks.
The presenter calls stacked post-purchase offers annoying to consumers — treat consumer-experience tolerance as a variable, and verify current one-click checkout capabilities with your platform.

cards.title: Anchor high then down-sell when sequencing post-purchase offers
cards.summary: Lead post-purchase with a higher-priced upsell and down-sell below it, because leading with the cheapest offer anchors prices low.
cards.use_when: Building or reordering a post-purchase upsell/down-sell sequence.
steps: Show a higher-value upsell first (source example: $50–60 post-purchase) to set the price anchor.
If the customer declines, down-sell them into a lower offer ($20–30).
If they accept the first offer, flow them to another upsell slightly lower than the first ($30–40).
If they accept that, flow them into a second down-sell; if they decline the first, likewise route them through the down-sells.
Avoid the common mistake of leading with the cheapest offer — the source says this anchors at the low price and makes every later higher-value offer look expensive.
caveats: Sequence length is a consumer-experience tradeoff; the presenter personally dislikes long chains but uses them as an advertiser.
Dollar values are source examples; set your anchors from your own AOV and margin data.

cards.title: Apply the five rules for in-cart upsells
cards.summary: Keep one offer per cart slot, prioritize relevance, high margin, simplicity and gross-margin-lift measurement.
cards.use_when: Designing the in-cart drawer upsell slot.
steps: One offer per slot in the drawer cart — the source warns multiple offers cause decision fatigue and lower take rates.
Prioritize relevancy over price: a good price on an irrelevant item won't be taken.
Favor high-margin SKs so the added gross profit is worth the slot (avoid items yielding only a few dollars).
Keep the in-cart offer easy to understand — you have roughly two to three seconds of legibility, so a simple flat discount usually works better here even though front-end offers can be complex.
Measure in-cart upsell success by gross margin lift, not AOV lift, to avoid over-prioritizing low-margin SKs.
Where an offer is congruent with what was bought, take rate is higher — let fit guide the pick before price.
caveats: The 'two to three seconds' timeframe is the source's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Relevance and margin can conflict; the source's instruction is to prefer the option that nets more incremental contribution profit.

cards.title: Use revenue per visit (RPV) to size the post-purchase opportunity
cards.summary: RPV = post-purchase revenue ÷ post-purchase funnel visits (or average upsell value × conversion rate), with a source-cited target of 10–15%.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a post-purchase upsell program is contributing enough incremental revenue.
steps: Compute RPV as post-purchase revenue captured divided by post-purchase funnel visits.
Alternatively compute it as average upsell value × conversion rate.
Interpret RPV as the extra dollars earned per person entering the post-purchase funnel.
Example: a $200 AOV with a 10% RPV yields $20 extra per order — the source frames this as a fast way to lift AOV if implemented well.
caveats: The '10 to 15%' figure is the source's stated target benchmark, not a universal standard.
The source itself notes the 10–15% AOV uplift is only realizable 'if implemented correctly' — treat it as a goal, not a promise.

cards.title: Structure gift-with-purchase offers that raise units per transaction without eroding margin
cards.summary: A cheap, relevant free gift can roughly double contribution margin and lower break-even ROAS, but only if the gift's perceived value is real.
cards.use_when: Building a multi-buy or bundle offer and choosing the free gift.
steps: Add a free secondary item on a multi-unit purchase only when you have a low-cost SK that pairs well (source example: buy two $50 towels, get a $4-cost bag free).

Model the economics including shipping/fulfillment. Source example: one towel CM ≈ $26.50, two-with-gift CM ≈ $53.50, with break-even ROAS falling from ~1.89 to ~1.87 — i.e., you can run at worse efficiency for roughly double the money.
To lift the gift's perceived value, sell it on-site and display the combined value — present '$160 discounted to $100' rather than 'spend $100, get a free bag.'
Only run the offer if the gift is something the customer actually wants — the source's core test is whether the customer cares, and margin math is worthless if they don't.

Layer offers only around the biggest customer objection: if buyers worry about durability, attach a lifetime guarantee to the higher-AOV offer rather than an irrelevant extra (the source calls out an irrelevant prize-pool example as a failure mode).
Always start offer design from customer surveys ('what held you back?'), not from your ideal margin structure.
caveats: The source's example numbers are illustrative and industry-specific; run your own math.
A lifetime guarantee is meaningless for consumables that are eaten or used up — match the guarantee to the product category.
Verify the operationally feasible gift and its COGS with your supplier before committing.

cards.title: Set tiered/threshold offers using the AOV distribution, not the average
cards.summary: Bimodal AOV distributions require offers targeted at each peak rather than one threshold set from the mean, which can leak margin without moving anyone.
cards.use_when: Designing threshold mechanics like free-shipping or spend-to-unlock for a catalog with varied order sizes.
steps: Chart the AOV distribution across all orders (histogram or line) instead of reading Shopify's single average-order-value figure.
Check whether it is bimodal (two peaks, common with large SK counts like fashion where carts vary) or unimodal (e.g., supplements where customers buy 30-day or 90-day supplies).
Identify the peaks and set a target offer to shift each peak up (e.g., free shipping at a threshold just above each peak), rather than a single threshold based on the mean.

Recognize the failure case: a mean-based threshold above the lower peak gives free shipping to everyone already spending more (pure margin loss) while the lower-peak group can't double their order to reach it — the source estimates only ~10% of customers are actually moved.
Layer mechanics — e.g., a gift with purchase for one peak and a different mechanic for the other — rather than one mechanism across the whole catalog.
caveats: The '~10% of customers' and '80% do this wrong' figures are the source's characterizations, not measured benchmarks.
Distribution shape should be recalculated as your catalog and offers change.

cards.title: Use flat discounting rarely and only for specific scenarios
cards.summary: Straight discounting is a legitimate mechanic only for high-gross-margin SKs or grade-C inventory, and should be used one to two times a year at most.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a site-wide or category discount promotion.
steps: Restrict straight discounting to two situations the source identifies: a few SKs with very high gross margin, or grade-C inventory you need to convert to cash.
Model AOV (and units per transaction) lift using prior discount performance so you don't over-discount and lose margin — find the point where UPT increases and contribution margin is maximized.
Model the target ROAS required at the new discount threshold, and sense-check whether that efficiency is realistically achievable.
Run these events rarely — one to two times per year per the source — because frequent discounting trains the existing and in-market customer base to always wait for a sale and erodes brand equity.
Judge the goal as converting unmoving stock into cash, not rescuing topline revenue; the source calls businesses that must discount to hit revenue targets structurally weaker.
caveats: The 1–2x/year frequency is the presenter's recommendation, not a universal rule.
Contribution margin impact is usually negative unless unit lift outweighs margin erosion — do the math before running it.

cards.title: Segment exit-intent offers by funnel stage
cards.summary: Browse, cart and checkout exits represent different intent levels, so give generous urgency to browsers, tiny offers to cart abandoners, and risk-reversal (not discounts) to checkout abandoners.
cards.use_when: Setting up exit-intent popups or abandoned-cart/checkout email and SMS flows.
steps: Split exits into three stages: browsing, added-to-basket, and reached-checkout.
For pure browsers (no commitment, still product-aware), be generous and add urgency to give a reason to buy.
For basket-abandoners (showing intent, may just need a day or two), avoid giving away all margin — offer only something small.

For checkout-abandoners, don't lead with a discount; instead use risk reversal or a shipping offer, because the source judges them likely to buy within a couple of days anyway and warns that discounting here surrenders margin unnecessarily.
The source is sceptical of browser-exit popups as gimmicky and says an abandoned-flow email sequence is an alternative — choose which to prioritise based on your flow data.
caveats: The 'likely to buy within 2–3 days' expectation is the presenter's assertion, not a measured figure.
Exit intent should be measured as a cohort to confirm the assumption holds for your store before relying on it.

cards.title: Select and iterate the right front-end offer via four diagnostic questions
cards.summary: Choose offers by gross margin floor, AOV distribution shape, single vs multi SKU, and repeat behaviour — then test, since only about 10 of 100 possible offers are good.
cards.use_when: Choosing which front-end acquisition offer to run for a product line or campaign.
steps: Q1 — What is the gross margin floor? Start by modelling the economics to see whether the offer improves profitability or just erodes margin.
Q2 — What does the AOV distribution look like? If two peaks, split offers across those thresholds; if one peak, focus on moving the core audience up (e.g., supplements: move 30-day to 90-day).

Q3 — Single hero SK or multiple SKs? With one SK lean on product repositioning first, then gift with purchase, and be disciplined with discounting; with multiple SKs you can use native bundles, cross-category upsells and threshold mechanics.

Q4 — What is the buyer's repeat behaviour? Use it to decide whether to build subscription offers into the front-end, discount structure, gift presentation and lock-in periods — or, if repeat is very low, to protect first-order margin hard.

After answering, recognise there are '100 different offers and probably 10 good ones' and no one can say which works best before in-market testing; set up dedicated landing pages to split-test offers.
Once you have an existing customer base, survey it repeatedly to iterate; the source notes large CPG brands often hold an offer static for 6–12 months while testing replacements on the side.
caveats: The '10 of 100' ratio and '6–12 months static' are the presenter's observations, not benchmarks.
Subscription and lock-in mechanics depend on your repeat behaviour; if repeat is minimal, first-order margin carries the business.

cards.title: Diagnose why front-end offers fail
cards.summary: Common failure modes: calling a bare discount an offer, miscalculating margin, using the same offer for new vs returning customers, mean-based thresholds, a wrong or uneconomic gift, an endless promo calendar, and blaming Q1 on seasonality.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a struggling or underperforming promotional calendar.
steps: Check if you're defaulting to a blank percentage discount and calling it an offer — that sidelines everything else the offer could do.
Check your margin calculation: does it include shipping, fulfilment and pick cost, and does it properly show the improved efficiency that bundles and higher UPT can unlock?
Check audience targeting: new-customer offers should optimise for first-purchase economics, while repeat offers should lock in cohorts for a sustained period — these are different mechanics.
Check thresholds: the source says ~80% of operators set them off the mean AOV instead of the distribution curve.
Check the gift: is it something customers actually care about, and does it materially change the economics? If not, the offer fails.

Check the promo calendar: an all-year 25-week rotation of category discounts is unsustainable; and treat Q1 as an offer-design opportunity rather than an unavoidable seasonal dip — it is also a good time to test offers given suppressed conversion rates and market sentiment.
caveats: The '~80%' and '25-week' figures are the source's characterisations, not measured statistics.
Q1 as a testing window assumes you can afford to run a test during slower periods.

cards.title: Plan discounting by modelling AOV lift and required efficiency
cards.summary: Undisciplined discounting erodes margin unless you model AOV/UPT lift from prior discounts and the ROAS needed at the new threshold.
cards.use_when: Planning a price promotion and its paid media efficiency.
steps: Before running a discount, model the AOV lift and units-per-transaction lift based on how previous discounts performed — this prevents over-discounting.
From that AOV lift, calculate the target return on ad spend needed to hit your profit-contribution target at the new discount threshold.
Sense-check reachability: is the required ROAS realistic for your account and channel mix? If not, adjust the discount depth or run the offer differently.
Use the same mechanics that guard margin during discounting — bundle economics, gift-with-purchase and threshold mechanics — so a discount doesn't stand alone.
Read the offer as one of the most important acquisition levers in the source's framing, not as a cost-cutting exercise.
caveats: The source notes it offers a companion discounting calculator externally; you would need to source or build your own equivalent and verify its assumptions.
This card is based on the presenter's framework, not an audited methodology — test assumptions on your own data.

cards.title: Design bundles across SKs and as repeated same-SKU offers
cards.summary: Bundles protect contribution margin but are fundamentally an easy offer; there is more upside in creatively combining mechanics rather than stopping at a basic SK bundle.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a straightforward multi-buy bundle vs a layered offer.
steps: Confirm the basic mechanics apply: a bundle works when you package different SKs together, or when you package the same SK multiple times (e.g., a buy-two-get-25%-off deal like a board-game offer).
Validate it only suits multi-SKU brands or consumable products where repeated purchase is plausible — a single non-consumable SK usually cannot bundle this way.
Accept that the bundle itself protects contribution margin but the source argues it is under-using offer potential because it is a simple, familiar mechanics.
Layer the bundle with other mechanics: gift with purchase, a threshold unlock, or a guarantee on the higher-AOV offer, so it does more than a flat multi-buy discount.
Follow the same discount economics as for straight discounting — the same margin and ROAS modelling applies to bundles.
caveats: The source's view that bundles are an 'easy' offer is an opinion — bundle-only strategies still work when they protect margin.
Layering mechanics increases comprehension cost at checkout; in-cart offers specifically should stay simple.

cards.title: Consolidation beats segmentation in Meta account structure
cards.summary: Fewer campaigns and adsets generally outperform highly segmented structures, because Meta chooses where to spend based on incremental returns and cross-ad sequencing, not the siloed per-ad metrics you see.
cards.use_when: Deciding campaign/adset structure for a paid social account.
steps: Start from the principle that fewer campaigns and adsets generally perform better — this replaced the 2018-era interest-segmentation orthodoxy after iOS 14 (the source says Meta reported losing ~30% of its targeting signal) and its AI retrieval improvements.

Recognise you see last-click attribution while Meta optimises across multi-touch attribution and a chain of impressions, so spend flows to ads that appear weak at the ad level if they participate in the purchase path.

Watch the breakdown effect: a placement or demographic breakdown can show higher ROAS yet receive less spend because Meta has tested pushing more spend there and found incremental ROI poor — most of the time trust Meta's distribution.

Consider that segmentation exists to serve business needs (separate business units, budget flows, reporting/KPIs) and accept that cross-campaign conversion data sharing is worse than at adset and ad level.

Reserve complex restructuring from placement or audience breakdowns for genuinely experienced media buyers — the source says beginners make worse decisions by over-segmenting on breakdowns they misread.
caveats: The source's claim that segmentation will 'always' lose to consolidation is the presenter's claim, hedged elsewhere as 'not necessarily the right thing to do'.
The platform's behaviour around interest targeting and retrieval changes over time — verify current Meta documentation and test on your own account.
This card reflects the source's Metas-specific view; other platforms may differ.

cards.title: Match Meta spend playbook and structure decisions to account size
cards.summary: The right account structure depends on spend level — the source frames three playbooks (under 50k, 50–250k, 250k+ per month) and notes media buying still matters at higher spend.
cards.use_when: Choosing how much structure and manual media buying effort to apply based on monthly ad spend.
steps: Identify your monthly spend band: under $50k, $50k–$250k, or $250k+ (source framing).
At low spend (source example: ~$100/day), don't expect media buying to be a major lever on account performance.
At high spend (source example: $100k–$300k per month), media buying can produce a meaningful efficiency lift if done correctly per the source.
Accept that there is no universal perfect account structure — the presenter states it varies by business, so design from your own constraints and goals.
Always be able to articulate why a campaign or adset exists, since the platform's structure needs a commercial rationale.
caveats: The efficiency lift figure (~10–20%) is the presenter's estimate, not a verified benchmark.
The specific spend bands are the presenter's playbook categories, not a rule imposed by the platform.

cards.title: Use broad targeting with creative-driven audience retrieval
cards.summary: Broad targeting lets the platform's retrieval system place creative by its understanding of the ad, clustering users in high-dimensional space rather than relying on interest labels that don't capture intent.
cards.use_when: Setting targeting for a new Meta campaign or testing whether to keep interest-based audiences.
steps: Load creative and leave targeting broad, then let the platform serve each creative to the audience it matches.

Understand the limitation of interest targeting: it is label-based and does not capture intent (the source's example — someone who says they hate dogs can be tagged as interested in dogs; the source cites a report that 30% of an interest group can be mis-assigned).
Think of broad targeting as scattering ads across a large vector space and following the clusters that buy, rather than proxying audiences with labels.
Expect ads to fatigue or campaigns to die during scaling because you move from a hyped-specific cluster into colder clusters where the creative is not convincing enough.
Treat interests as generally flawed but not absolutely dead, and decide per business — the source hedge is 'generally speaking'.
caveats: The 30% figure is attributed by the source to an external report and is not verified here.
Interest targeting behaviour and Meta's retrieval systems change over time — verify current platform documentation and test on your own account before switching.

cards.title: Diagnose scaling death and ad fatigue with the cluster model
cards.summary: Ads fatigue when scaling pushes spend into colder clusters where the creative no longer convinces — the source frames this as the core limit on scaling a winning campaign.
cards.use_when: Managing a scaling campaign that is decaying or losing efficiency.
steps: Start from the idea that broad targeting sprinkles your ad across users who cluster by behaviour and that buying initially comes from hotspots.
When you scale, the platform widens the served area around the hotspot — colder audiences get shown the ad and often don't convert because the ad is not persuasive enough for them.
Treat this as the structural cause of campaign decay and ad fatigue rather than a simple metric problem.
Respond with stronger creative (the source's model treats creative comprehension/conviction as the real gate on how far you can scale) rather than only restructuring spend.
Use broad targeting as the base and validate which clusters respond by watching where conversions concentrate.
caveats: The vector/10,000-dimension cluster model is the presenter's explanatory analogy, not a literal platform description.
Colder-audience expansion may still be profitable in some cases; the source says it is the reason most campaigns die, not that all scaling is unprofitable.

cards.title: Set cost caps and bidding at the adset level, not the ad level
cards.summary: Bidding and optimisation are inherited from the adset, so ad-level ROAS tells you what you see, not where the platform places the bid.
cards.use_when: Configuring bid strategy or cost caps in a Meta campaign and interpreting ad-level reporting.
steps: Understand that cost caps and complex bidding approaches belong at the adset level, because adset is where bidding and optimisation are inherited.
Read ad-level ROAS as last-click and ad-level attribution, not as the target Meta is optimising toward — the platform optimises toward the adset CPA target.
When an ad looks weak, check whether it is participating in a click/impression sequence rather than assuming it deserves to be switched off.
Consider the breakdown effect before making restructuring decisions off placement or audience breakdown data.
For beginners, avoid making structural changes based on complex breakdowns — the source says this tends to produce worse performance than trusting the platform.
caveats: Platform interfaces and default settings change, so verify current bidding and cost cap configuration options in the Meta interface.
The source's advice on trusting the platform applies specifically to lower-experience operators; the source allows for expert-level restructuring.
